issues.issue: The acceptance form describes the Memorandum of Agreement as "dated December , 1991," whereas the Memorandum was made and executed in May 1992 (c061 and the letters are dated May 16, 1992). The mis-dating leaves it uncertain which instrument the employee is accepting a buyout under.

The form lets the employee designate a person to receive the remaining buyout amount, while Attachment A, Schedule of Payments 3 (c045) directs the unpaid balance to the employee's estate. The designation and the estate provision cannot both govern.

Attachment B extends the offer to those on the Group I list "effective the date of ratification," while the Memorandum's definition (c014) requires presence on the list both at signing and at ratification. The two eligibility tests differ for the same group.
"[I]nterest at prevailing market interest rates" identifies no rate source, annuity term or measurement date. The economic content of the annuity election is unfixed.

The balance goes to "the individual's estate," but the Attachment B Notice of Termination (c060) invites the individual to name someone to whom the remaining buyout is to be paid. The two payment directions conflict.
The offer stays open 45 days "commencing promptly after ratification," which supplies no ascertainable opening or closing date. "Promptly" is the only measure of the trigger.

The Attachment B acceptance form refers to a Memorandum of Agreement "dated December , 1991," while the Memorandum bears a May 1992 date. The date is a mechanical error about the very instrument being accepted.
The beneficiary designation on the form conflicts with Attachment B, Schedule of Payments 3 (c056), which directs any unpaid balance to the individual's estate. Which controls on death is unresolved.

Guaranteed Employees are "those Regular Situation Holders to be identified on Attachments '1' and '2'," lists that are neither annexed nor described by any criterion. The class of beneficiaries of the employment guarantee is left to be created after the fact.

"[G]uaranteed the opportunity to work five straight time shifts per week" does not say whether the guarantee is one of pay when work is not offered or merely of an offer the employee must accept. "Opportunity" carries both meanings and fixes the guarantee's value.

Appendix A repeatedly says "this Agreement," which may mean Appendix A itself or the Memorandum it is appended to, and the same sentence makes the guarantee both effective on completion of Memorandum paragraph 4B and surviving "the expiration of this Agreement." Which instrument's expiration is meant decides how long the Attachment "1" guarantees run.

The Attachment "2" guarantee ends at "the expiration date of the current Collective Bargaining Agreement," a phrase that may mean the March 30, 1993 expiry recited in the opening clause (c001) or that Agreement as there extended to March 30, 2000. The guarantee's duration turns entirely on that term.

The right to "utilize fully" Guaranteed Employees "in inverse seniority order" before hiring others sits against paragraph B (c062), which guarantees each Guaranteed Employee five straight-time shifts a week. Calling up the most junior first can leave senior guaranteed employees short of their guarantee.

Guarantees are confined to persons listed on Attachments "1" and "2" "except for Eligible Group I Employees who obtain guarantees pursuant to paragraph 4B" of the Memorandum, while paragraph 4B (c021) says those employees' guarantee is "governed by the terms of Appendix A" — which limits itself to the listed individuals. The two provisions refer to each other without fixing the content of the Group I guarantee.

Suspension of the guarantee depends on the delivery department's operations being suspended "in circumstances under which RSH's are not entitled to be paid under the Collective Bargaining Agreement," a condition defined only by an external document not reproduced here. Which shutdowns qualify cannot be determined from this instrument.

"[P]ermanent suspension of the Newspaper" identifies neither the publication nor who determines permanence, and no notice or verification mechanism is supplied. A prolonged but arguably temporary shutdown falls in the gap.

The general words are "any employee who terminates employment for any reason," yet the enumerated instances include discharge, death and permanent disability — none of them acts of the employee. The list contradicts the general term it is said to illustrate.

The Times may terminate the guarantees for "any violation" of the No-Strike clause, while paragraph 7C of the Memorandum (c033) expressly releases the Union from that clause on the employer's non-compliance with an award. A work stoppage lawful under 7C would still forfeit the guarantees under this clause.

The Union's option is triggered by a "wage package" agreed with another union, and the letter never says whether pension and welfare contributions form part of a "wage package." The predecessor 1987 provision used "wage and benefit package," making the narrowed term's scope a live question.

The right is triggered by agreement with "any labor organization" followed by a closed parenthetical list of nine named unions. Whether the parenthetical exhausts the trigger or merely illustrates it is a general-versus-specific problem.

Disputes go to "the Contract's grievance and arbitration procedure," while paragraph 2 of the Memorandum (c008) vests all disputes over the Agreement in the Merits Arbitrator selected under its own procedure. Which machinery hears a most-favored-wage dispute is unsettled between the two.

The Times must file the vacatur papers "promptly upon notification" of ratification, with no outside date and no specified form of notification. What counts as prompt, and as notification, is left open.

This letter excludes 43rd Street and the staging facility from every reference to "new and rebuilt facilities," while paragraph 1A of the Memorandum (c004) applies the contract as modified at "any new or rebuilt facility" within the NMDU's jurisdiction. The scope of section 1 cannot be fixed without reconciling the two.

The letter freezes forty current SNBD finishing times "throughout the duration of this contract," while paragraph 6 of the Memorandum (c027) makes the reorganization "subject only to" the forty-route minimum. The letter adds a limitation that paragraph 6 says does not exist.

The letter funds welfare shortfalls out of the paragraph 3.A.(3) contributions and then requires "additional contributions" if those are insufficient, whereas paragraph 3.A.(3) (c015) states that its contributions are "in lieu of and not in addition to" what the Agreement would otherwise require. Whether The Times owes more than the 450-FTE minimum turns on reconciling them.

The obligation is measured by "shift contributions needed to maintain benefit status," a standard set by the Pension Fund's own rules and nowhere stated in this instrument. The size of the employer's separate contribution is not ascertainable from the letter.

The whole funding obligation is conditioned on the individuals' "willingness ... to avail themselves of all work opportunities that may exist at The New York Times," a condition with no test, no procedure for proving it, and no indication whether one refusal defeats the obligation for all. "All work opportunities" is also unbounded as to location, shift and classification.

The letter raises the minimum FTE contributions by the number of FTEs employed "in excess of 370," while paragraph 3-A(3) (c015) sets the minimum at 450 FTEs — so employment of, say, 400 FTEs would produce a 480-FTE contribution obligation. How the 370 threshold works against the 450 floor is not explained.

Dedicated school and college drivers are assigned "a regular shift time of 2:30 to 9:30 a.n.," yet on suspension or abolition of the route "the driver's start time will revert to 11:30 p.m." — a time the clause never established. What the driver reverts to, and on what notice, is unclear.

"[E]very effort within its control" to protect the NMDU's jurisdiction against "hootlegging" operations supplies neither a standard of effort nor a definition of the target conduct. Both the obligation and its object are undefined.
The committee is composed of two representatives from each side with no chair, tie-breaker or decision rule. Deadlock is unaddressed and the committee's output is not made binding on anyone.

The committee is "specifically charged with administering the transfer process," without saying whether that gives it authority to decide transfers or only to implement decisions The Times makes. "Administering" carries both meanings against the Times' discretion elsewhere in the package.

The 1996 contributions are reduced from the 450-FTE obligation and "[s]aid reductions will be evenly distributed throughout the calendar years 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995" — reductions to years that will already have closed before the 1996 contributions are made. How a future measurement is spread over past contribution years is not explained.

The reduction cuts into the 450-Full-Time-Equivalent minimum fixed by paragraph 3-A(3) (c015), which is expressed as a firm minimum for 1992-1995. Whether the minimum or the reduction controls those years is a direct clash.

The parties promise to "take the steps necessary to effectuate amendments to the Health and Welfare Plan" required by paragraph 3-A(3) (c015), but the Plan is a trusteed fund whose contributions are set by the collective bargaining agreements and trust instrument, not by these two parties. What amendments are "necessitated," and whether the promisors can deliver them, only appears when the instruments are read together.

The clause turns on "the most junior qualified situation holder" without any definition of "qualified" or of the pool from which juniority is measured. Who may be compelled to take an Edison situation is therefore contestable.

This paragraph requires at least four days' notice before assignment, while the following paragraph (c088) requires the Chapel Chairman to produce a volunteer within three days and the volunteer to fill the situation within seven days of notification. The two timetables cannot be run together for the same vacancy.

The volunteer procedure must precede the junior-assignment procedure, yet its three-day and seven-day steps are inconsistent with the four days' notice that c087 requires before a junior holder is assigned, and it ends by permanently assigning the junior holder anyway. Sequencing the two paragraphs requires construction.

The exception depends on a vacancy "foreseen to be of two (2) weeks or less duration," without saying by whom the foresight is exercised or what happens when it proves wrong. The exception is thus effectively self-judged.

The Times is given a bare "option to fill any vacancies created" by a junior assignment, while the same letter (c086) commits the parties to staff vacant, newly created or temporary situations expeditiously. Whether the option overrides that commitment for the knock-on vacancy is unaddressed.

The NMDU "may, within 72 hours, discuss the possibility of employment opportunities," without identifying what event starts the 72 hours or imposing any duty on The Times beyond discussion. Both the trigger and the substance of the right are indeterminate.

The award of a named dispatcher position to M. Santor by side letter sits against the bidding and seniority-based assignment machinery preserved elsewhere in the package (c086-c088 and the Contract's bid procedures). Whether other situation holders' bid rights yield to this individual award is not addressed.
The letter commits M. Santor to withdraw his grievance "with prejudice" although he is not a signatory to it and no mechanism binds him. Who must act, and what follows if he does not, is unstated.
